title: Environmental view and color for a simulated telemarketing task
research_question: To determine the effects of task type or a break, environmental color, and environmental view on mood, satisfaction, motivation, and performance in a simulated telemarketing task.

participants.description: Experiment 1: 128 undergraduate students (32 male, 96 female), ages 18-25 (median 19) from a mid-sized, private mid-western university in the USA. Experiment 2: 128 undergraduate students (36 male, 92 female), ages 17-28 (median 19) from a mid-sized, private mid-western university in the USA.
participants.recruitment: Volunteered for course credit in psychology courses.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Partitioned workspaces (carrels) painted either dark red (Munsell 5R 5/8) or light blue (Munsell 10B 7/6). Panels extended 61 cm up from desk top. Workspaces were 24 cm apart.
Scenic picture (20.3 cm × 25.4 cm) of a sunset behind mountains viewed across a lake, placed centered just above the computer (39.5 cm above desk top) vs. no picture.

Scripted audiotapes of telemarketing reservation sessions. Experiment 1: Low demand (2 sessions, 6.75 min quiet between 1st and 4th, 3 min after 4th) vs. High demand (5 sessions, 3s space between sessions). Experiment 2: High demand (5 sessions, 3s space between sessions) with or without a 90s quiet break between sessions 3 and 4.

measures.instrument: Multiple Affect Adjective Check List (MAACL) state form (Anxiety, Hostility, Depression scores combined)
Multiple Affect Adjective Check List (MAACL) state form (Positive Affect, Sensation Seeking scores combined)
2-item 5-point Likert-type questionnaire (alpha=0.90 in Exp 1, alpha=0.86 in Exp 2)
3-item 5-point Likert-type questionnaire (alpha=0.72 in Exp 1, alpha=0.54 in Exp 2)
2-item 5-point Likert-type questionnaire (alpha=0.70 in Exp 1, alpha=0.68 in Exp 2)
5-item 5-point Likert-type questionnaire (alpha=0.82 in Exp 1, alpha=0.83 in Exp 2)
3 individual items from 5-point Likert-type questionnaire (alpha=0.21 in Exp 1, alpha=0.26 in Exp 2)

measures.construct: Desire to view or be viewed by another student
measures.instrument: 2-item 5-point Likert-type questionnaire (alpha=0.89 in Exp 1, alpha=0.80 in Exp 2)
Computerized scoring of entries to reservation forms (typographical, omission, wrong entry, blank, miscellaneous errors)

measures.construct: Looking about the environment when not entering data
measures.instrument: 2 individual items from 5-point Likert-type questionnaire (alpha=0.37 in Exp 2)

findings.quote: In contrast, individuals in the red environment had a significantly greater desire to view or to be viewed by another... when there was no picture than when there was a picture.

findings.antecedent: Blue environmental color AND scenic picture present (Experiment 1)

mechanisms: Comparative process: individuals compare their current task situation with ideas generated from the scenic picture or environmental color, which can make the task seem more boring or demanding, or provide a sense of being away.
Restorative function: scenic pictures and calming colors (blue) can help individuals fend off distractions and restore attention.
Stimulation/Calming: Red is stimulating, blue is calming, and these effects can interact with task demands and other environmental features.
Attentional fatigue: High demand tasks lead to fatigue over time, which can be modulated by environmental factors.
implementation_implications: For high demand tasks in stimulating (red) environments, providing breaks or scenic pictures can help control errors.
Calming environments (blue) might be detrimental for low demand/boring tasks, potentially increasing errors over time.
Environmental design elements (color, views) can influence desire for social interaction and perceived privacy, which may be important for telemarketing environments.

limitations: Short duration of the task (15 minutes) may have limited the impact on mood, satisfaction, and motivation.
Participants were students receiving course credit, not hired telemarketers, which may affect motivation and task engagement.
Lighting levels were not consistently measured across all conditions and may have confounded some results, particularly in the blue carrels.
Individual color preferences were not assessed and could impact results.
The specific scenic picture used may not generalize to other types of views or pictures.
The high demand task might not have been demanding enough to fully elicit attentional fatigue effects.
